title: Locality of deep thermalisation through the lens of entanglement teleportation
authors: Saptarshi Mandal, Alan Sherry, Sthitadhi Roy
abstract: Deep thermalisation characterises the emergence of universal quantum state ensembles on subsystems due to projective measurements on their complement. We study the notion of locality, or lack thereof, in this phenomenon by considering a subsystem partitioned into two disjoint subregions which remain causally disconnected at all times under unitary dynamics. We show that the onset of deep thermalisation in this geometry is fundamentally bounded by measurement-induced entanglement teleportation between the subregions. While measurements on the environment generate entanglement across the disconnected partitions -- suggesting an apparent non-locality -- we demonstrate that generic locally interacting systems exhibit an emergent locality. Specifically, the timescales for both deep thermalisation and entanglement teleportation scale logarithmically with the distance separating the subregions. Exceptions to this include special circuits where the randomness of the measurement outcomes is perfectly transmitted to the ensemble of states of the subsystem, conditioned on the outcomes; in such cases the timescale for deep thermalisation is finite leading to genuine non-locality.
summary: This paper rigorously examines the concept of locality during deep thermalization by comparing entanglement teleportation to state ensemble convergence. It shows that while measurements can induce apparent non-local effects, generic local interactions enforce an emergent locality characterized by logarithmic time scaling with distance. This provides a fundamental constraint on how fast quantum information can spread in realistic physical systems.
main_problem: The study investigates whether deep thermalization, a process driven by projective measurements on an environment, exhibits emergent locality when the system is partitioned into causally disconnected regions.
main_result: In generic locally interacting systems, both deep thermalization and entanglement teleportation exhibit timescales that scale logarithmically with the spatial separation ($\propto \ln L$), demonstrating emergent locality. Genuine non-locality only appears in special circuits where randomness transmission is perfect.
method: The analysis employs theoretical tools including moment calculations ($\Delta^{(k)}$), bipartite purity measures ($\delta P(k)$), and comparing results from minimal models, spatially extended brickwork circuits, and Random Tensor Networks (RTNs).
model_or_system: The work considers quantum systems undergoing unitary evolution followed by projective measurements. Models range from simple minimal setups to 1D locally interacting chains with specific Hamiltonians ($H = \sum [u_j \otimes u_{j+1}] e^{-i	au H} [\dots]$).
key_observables: Deep thermalization deviation ($\Delta^{(k)}$), entanglement teleportation measure ($\delta P(k)$), and bipartite purity (Pann).
important_parameters: System size/separation ($L$ or $L_R$), measurement depth, and the scaling of timescales with separation ($\ln L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes generic local interactions; perfect non-locality is restricted to special circuits transmitting randomness perfectly.
figures_summary: Figures show numerical decay rates for $\Delta^{(k)}$ and $\delta P(k)$ in the minimal model, demonstrating exponential decay. For the brickwork circuit, data collapse onto universal curves confirms the $\ln L$ scaling of the characteristic timescale $t^*$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing diagnostics ($\Delta^{(k)}, \delta P(k)$) and comparing them to Haar limits. It then analyzes a minimal model showing fast thermalization, before moving to spatially extended circuits where it establishes the $\ln L$ scaling characteristic of emergent locality.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body systems, providing quantitative bounds on how quickly quantum information spreads and thermalizes across spatially separated regions, which is crucial for understanding quantum computation limits.
